matthew-henson.excerpt: In April 1909 he stood at, or very near, the top of the world. Then he spent 23 years as a customs clerk.
sections: Cabin boy

Matthew Henson was born in Maryland on 8 August 1866, Bowdoin College says; National Geographic gives 6 August. He was an orphan by eleven. At twelve or thirteen he went to sea as a cabin boy aboard the Katie Hines, out of Baltimore, and the ship's captain taught him to read and write. Later he worked as a clerk in a Washington hat shop, and in 1887 the shop's owner recommended him to a naval officer who needed a valet for a surveying trip to Nicaragua. The officer was Robert Peary.
Seven expeditions

In 1890 Henson went with Peary to Greenland for the first time. Between 1891 and 1902 he spent seven years in the Arctic, and by Bowdoin's count made seven expeditions in all, covering some 9,000 miles by dog sled across northern Greenland and Ellesmere Island. He was the only member of Peary's party who learned to speak Inuktitut, and the Inuit respected him for his hunting and his sledging. Peary said he was more of an Eskimo than some of them; a remark often quoted, that Peary could not get along without him, comes through a single magazine writer and is not repeated as a quotation here.
6 April 1909

In the summer of 1908 Peary and Henson sailed north on the Roosevelt with 22 Inuit men, 17 women, 10 children and 246 dogs. In February 1909 they left Cape Sheridan, on Ellesmere Island, and Inuit teams laid the trail and supply caches towards the Pole. On 6 April 1909, with four Inuit companions, Henson and Peary reached their final camp. Peary announced that they had reached the North Pole.

Whether they reached the exact Pole is still debated. Henson's own account says he arrived at the camp about 45 minutes before Peary and judged by dead reckoning that he was at the Pole, and that Peary was angry about it and scarcely spoke to him afterwards. That rests on Henson's account alone, so it is not stated here as fact.
The Customs House

Peary received the fame. Henson's welcome home was, in Bowdoin's words, distinctly cool. In 1912 he published his own book, A Negro Explorer at the North Pole, and he spent more than two decades as a messenger and clerk at the Customs House in New York, retiring at seventy on a pension of 1,020 dollars a year.

Recognition came late. In 1937 the Explorers Club admitted him. He received honorary degrees from Howard University and Morgan College, and President Eisenhower honoured him at the White House. Donald MacMillan, who had been on the 1909 expedition, wrote that Henson went to the Pole with Peary because he was a better man than any of the rest of them.
Arlington

Matthew Henson died in 1955. In 1988, after a campaign by the Harvard professor S. Allen Counter, he and his wife Lucy were reburied at Arlington National Cemetery, near Peary. In 1996 the Navy named a survey ship for him, and in 2000 the National Geographic Society awarded him its highest honour, the Hubbard Medal, 91 years after the expedition; its president called the award long overdue.

muhammad-ali.excerpt: On 28 April 1967 his name was called three times, and three times he did not step forward. They took his title that same day.
sections: Cassius Clay

He was born Cassius Clay in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1942. At eighteen he won Olympic gold in Rome. In 1964, at 22, he beat Sonny Liston and became heavyweight champion of the world, and soon afterwards he joined the Nation of Islam and took the name Muhammad Ali. That same year he failed the army's entrance test, Sports Illustrated says because of dyslexia; in 1966 the army lowered its standard, and he became eligible for the draft.
Houston, 28 April 1967

On 28 April 1967, at the induction centre in Houston, his name was called. He did not step forward. It was called three times, and after a formal warning of the consequences he still did not move. He said his religion would not allow him to fight in the war in Vietnam. The same day, boxing's authorities stripped him of his title and suspended his licence. The famous lines he is often quoted as saying about the war appear in different wordings in different sources, so none is quoted here.
Five years and ten thousand dollars

On 20 June 1967 a jury convicted him of refusing induction. The sentence was five years in prison and a 10,000-dollar fine. He stayed free while he appealed, but he could not box. For three and a half years, at the peak of his career, he was out of the ring. The lower courts rejected his appeals without explaining why.
He regained a licence in 1970 and returned on 26 October that year, knocking out Jerry Quarry in Atlanta. On 8 March 1971 he lost for the first time, to Joe Frazier, over fifteen rounds in New York.
Eight to nothing

His case, Clay v. United States, reached the Supreme Court in 1971. Justice Thurgood Marshall took no part, because he had been Solicitor General when the case began. According to the journalists Bob Woodward and Scott Armstrong, the justices first voted five to three against Ali, and Justice John Harlan, assigned to write the opinion, changed his mind after a clerk gave him a book about Malcolm X; that account rests on their reporting. What is certain is the result: on 28 June 1971 the Court overturned the conviction, eight to nothing. Asked if he would sue, Ali said he could not condemn the government for doing what it thought was right.
Kinshasa
In 1974, in Kinshasa, Zaire, Ali beat George Foreman and became heavyweight champion of the world again. He died in 2016. They took his title. He took it back.
